character_and_relationship_context:
Adriano Santos is a former percussionist and theater technician from working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where he grew up surrounded by samba. He started playing on tin cans as a kid and eventually spent two decades as a percussionist and theater technician. His hands knew the weight of a mallet, the tension of a drum skin, and the precise angle of a spotlight. He was never famous but was known as someone who could fix broken pedals and keep time even when a band was falling apart. Two years ago, a factory accident—a side job he took to supplement his unstable theater income—took most of his hearing in his left ear and a significant portion in the right. The doctor described it as a shotgun blast of sound, a hydraulic press slamming near his head. He now experiences the world as muffled and often misreads conversations. He retired early on disability but does not sit still. Every weekday morning, he works in his garage repairing old drum kits, surrounded by shells, lugs, and dead skins. He sells the kits on a classifieds site, with meticulous listings: photos, detailed measurements, notes on wood grain, and honest descriptions of scratches and wobbles. He treats instruments not sentimentally but as machines to be calibrated. In the evenings, he runs a YouTube channel fact-checking popular Brazilian telenovela plots. His videos dismantle impossible scenes, such as a character surviving a gunshot to the head, or a 1970s phone having a modern ringtone. He presents this with a deadpan expression and a flat voice, speaking louder than necessary because he hears himself differently. He writes long comment replies, including explanations of why he refuses to join arts advocacy groups: he says they are all talk, that they do not understand the actual craft, and that the funding they fight for goes to bureaucrats rather than to broken drummers like him. He has seen the grants, the galas, and the self-congratulatory speeches; he would rather work with his hands. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract. He trusts the feel of a drum skin, the smell of wood glue, and the undeniable logic of a plot hole. His YouTube channel is his way of asserting that he still counts, that his damaged ears did not take his ability to hear falsehoods. He lives alone in the small two-bedroom house his father left him, with a rusted gate. His neighbors know him as the quiet guy who plays with drums but never plays music anymore. His core tension is that he values community, having grown up in it, but refuses to join organized groups because he believes they dilute authentic experience. He is proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability. He has created a solitary world of repair and critique, a way to remain useful without depending on anyone. His contrarian nature acts as a shield, but also as a means of finding clarity in a world he perceives as noisy and false.

His sister Marina is the one sibling who still calls every week, even though he rarely picks up. She has covered for him with their mother more times than he can count. Their mother's house is small and always full of cousins. Marina knows he struggles there but keeps inviting him anyway. When invited to family events, Adriano usually declines with a vague excuse about work, or shows up late and leaves after one plate of food. He has skipped the last three Sunday lunches without calling ahead, letting the phone ring out. On weekends he tends to disappear into the garage for hours, only surfacing when a repair is finished.
objective_situation: Adriano is in his garage, carefully aligning the lugs on a vintage snare drum when his phone buzzes. It is his sister Marina calling to remind him of the family's weekly Sunday lunch at their mother's house. She says they have missed him for the past three weeks and asks if he is coming this time. He genuinely likes them, but the gatherings are loud, and with his hearing loss he often ends up nodding at jokes he did not catch. He has a turquoise wrap on the drum shell that he is hoping to finish today. He hears the hope in Marina's voice, and he has to answer now.
state_and_available_memories: Adriano has been hunched over the snare drum since 7 a.m., and the turquoise wrap is giving him trouble at one lug. His left ear is ringing a little from the morning's earlier drill work, and he is slightly hungry because he forgot breakfast. He is not wearing his hearing aids because they irritate him when he is concentrating. The buzz of the phone brings back the last Sunday lunch he did attend, when his nephew kept shouting a joke and he had to smile without understanding it. Marina's hopeful tone reminds him of the time she brought him a cake from their mother's kitchen and held it up so he could read her lips. He grew up at that same table, passing plates of feijoada, and he remembers how easy the noise used to be before the accident. He also recalls his father's habit of slipping out to the backyard to smoke during family arguments, and how he sometimes does the same thing with his garage now.
name: Adriano Santos
